readerTitle: Why an 8% franchise fee can take half your profit
caseNote: 가상 사례 (청소 서비스, 샌드위치 가게) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 프랜차이즈 수수료는 매출이 아니라 이익과 비교하고, '이 시스템 없이 나는 얼마나 팔 수 있나'를 묻는다.
misconception: 매출의 8% 수수료는 이익의 8% 정도만 가져간다. 유명 브랜드를 달면 언제나 더 안전하고 더 많이 번다.

sources.text: 프랜차이즈의 일반 구조 (가맹비, 매출 기준 로열티, 광고 분담금)

factChecks.note: 손익 동일 지점: $28,000 ÷ 0.15 = $186,667(약 $187,000). 비용 비율이 같다는 단순화 가정이며, 실제로는 가맹 본부의 공동 구매 등으로 비용 구조가 다를 수 있음을 6·7번 카드에서 언급.
로열티가 보통 이익이 아닌 매출 기준으로 부과된다는 일반적 설명이 맞는지, 수수료율이 브랜드마다 크게 다르다는 점을 게시 전 확인. 특정 국가의 가맹 법규는 다루지 않음.

cards.title: Why an 8% franchise fee can take half your profit
body: Two home-cleaning businesses work the same town. Each brings in $400,000 a year. Same crews, same vans, same kind of customers.
One wears a franchise brand and pays 8% of its sales to head office. The other is independent. 8% sounds modest. Watch where it comes from.

image.label: Two identical cleaning vans, one with a generic brand badge
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 같은 모양의 청소 서비스 밴 두 대가 나란히 서 있음. 한 대에는 가상의 프랜차이즈 배지(별 모양 등 일반 도형), 다른 한 대는 손으로 쓴 동네 상호 느낌. 실제 브랜드 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: How much of your profit does 8% take?
body: The franchise takes 8% of sales: a 6% royalty plus a 2% marketing fund. Before those fees, the business keeps 15% of sales as profit after staff, supplies, vans and insurance.
What share of that profit goes to the fees?

options.feedback: That would be true if the fee came out of profit. It comes out of sales, before you've paid anyone else.
Right instinct that it bites harder than it sounds. The real figure is worse.
Yes. Fees of 8 cents per dollar of sales, against 15 cents of profit, take about 53% of what you'd keep. Next card shows it.

cards.title: Follow the franchise owner's year.
body: The independent owner keeps the full **$60,000**. Same sales, same work. The franchise owner keeps less than half of that.

cards.title: Franchise vs independent
body: A **franchise** rents you a proven business system: a known name, methods, training and supplier deals. You pay an upfront fee and an ongoing share of sales.
An independent business builds its own system. It keeps all the profit, and carries all the risk of figuring things out.
Because franchise fees usually come from sales, the honest comparison is fees against **profit**.

image.label: A boxed kit labeled brand, playbook, training, suppliers, handed over for a slice of a coin
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 'Brand', 'Playbook', 'Training', 'Supplier deals' 라벨이 붙은 상자 꾸러미, 오른쪽에 동전 더미에서 한 조각이 잘려 나가는 모습. 둘 사이에 교환 화살표. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: How much would you sell without them?
body: The franchise owner keeps 7 cents per dollar of sales. The independent keeps 15 cents.

So an independent selling just **$187,000** a year would earn the same $28,000. The franchise only pays off if, without the brand and system, you'd sell less than half as much, or run at much higher costs.
That's the number to estimate before signing.

image.label: Two bars: franchise at $400,000 and independent at $187,000 earn the same
image.brief: 막대 2개 비교. 'Franchise: $400,000 in sales'와 'Independent: $187,000 in sales'. 두 막대 위에 같은 크기의 'Owner keeps $28,000' 동전 아이콘. 짧은 막대가 같은 결과를 낸다는 점 강조.

cards.title: The fee buys most when you know least.
body: A franchise system is worth more to some owners than others. It tends to earn its fee when:
list: You're new to the trade and would make costly early mistakes
Customers search for the brand by name
The playbook, tools or supplier deals would take you years to build
cards.callout: If you already know the trade and your local reputation wins the work, you may be paying for things you have.
cards.softwareNote: Selling through a platform or app marketplace that takes a cut of every sale is a similar trade: you rent customers and tools for a share of revenue. Judge that cut against your profit, not your revenue.

cards.title: The yearly math leaves things out.
body: Upfront fees, required fit-outs and approved suppliers add costs on top of the royalty. Contracts can also limit your territory, prices, what you sell and whether you can renew or sell the business.
On the other side, the independent numbers assume you actually build a working system. Many owners don't, and a slow first year is a real cost.
Don't trust anyone's sales forecast alone. Ask existing owners, franchised and independent, what they really earn.

cards.title: Now it's a sandwich shop.
body: You've run kitchens for ten years and know local suppliers well. You expect $500,000 in sales and 12% profit before any fees. A sandwich franchise asks for 8% of sales in ongoing fees.

options.text: Sign. A known brand is the safer bet
options.feedback: Fees of $40,000 would take two-thirds of your $60,000 profit. You'd be paying mostly for experience and supplier ties you already have.

options.text: Go independent, and pay once for the specific gaps, like a till system or a brand designer
options.feedback: You keep the full profit and buy only the parts of a system you lack. The trade-off: you carry the risk that your own brand grows slowly.

options.text: Sign, but try to negotiate the fee down to 6%
options.feedback: A lower fee helps, but standard fees may not move much, and even 6% would take half your profit for help you don't really need.

cards.title: A franchise fee is the price of a system. Weigh it against profit, not sales.
body: Divide the fee by your profit, then ask how much you'd sell without the brand. The franchise wins only when that gap is bigger than the fee.
**Try it today:** take any deal where someone keeps a share of your sales, such as a franchise, platform or distributor. Divide their cut by your profit margin.
